scenario: AITA for insisting that my son’s therapist tells me why my son wants to see him. | My son [17] was always a normal boy, with many friends, very active and didn’t seam to have any kind of problem. But one day we he told us he needed to go see a therapist. We were really surprised by that, we never thought he will ask us something like that. We ask him why but he didn’t want to tell us. We were worried so we send him to a therapist and now he goes once a week. In our eyes he is still the same kid that before. We tried to think about things that he may have. We thought maybe he is bulimic or anorexic ( as he is very thin ) but he isn’t that skinny and those things tend to affect women, not men. We thought of depression but that also doesn’t seem very likely. We decided that theorizing wouldn’t give us an answer so we ask his therapist and refused, saying that he couldn’t say what my son told him. I told him that we didn’t want the specifics but at least the reason why he goes to therapy. But he refused again. We try to insist many times but he didn’t give up. And the day after, our son come to us and tell us that he know that we insisted on knowing why he wants therapy ( we don’t know if the therapist told him or maybe he hear us talking about it in the house ) and insulted us. He didn’t talk to us for the rest of the day. Now, we know that insist to know wasn’t the best idea but we are his parents and we deserve to know. We really are assholes?

message.reasoning:
The scenario describes parents insisting that their son's therapist disclose why their son is in therapy, despite the therapist's ethical obligation to maintain confidentiality. The therapist refuses, and the son becomes upset, feeling his privacy has been violated. The parents believe they have a right to know as parents.

The key ethical issue here is patient confidentiality. The therapist is bound by professional ethics (and likely legal requirements) to keep the client's information private, unless there is a risk of harm to self or others. The son is 17, which in many jurisdictions is considered a minor, but the age of majority is typically 18. However, even for minors, therapists often maintain confidentiality, especially regarding sensitive issues, and may share only with parental consent or if there is a danger. The parents' insistence on knowing the reason, despite the therapist's refusal, violates the son's right to privacy and could damage trust. The son's reaction (insulting, not talking) indicates he feels betrayed. The parents' belief that they "deserve to know" as parents is not absolute; the son's autonomy and confidentiality are important, especially as he is approaching adulthood. The therapist's refusal is ethically correct. The parents' actions are morally unacceptable because they disregard their son's privacy and the therapeutic relationship.

Thus, the action (insisting that the therapist disclose the reason) is morally unacceptable.
